lines.text: Later that night, one of the children woke up crying. Then another. Then all six.
Will the Academy be cold?
I don't know.
Can you sing something? Mama always sings.
I don't really know any songs.
But I hummed anyway. A tune I didn't remember ever learning. Slow and low, like wind going round a chimney.
One by one, they fell asleep. And in the doorway, Bram had gone as white as snow.
Bram?
He looked like he'd seen a ghost.
It's just a song.
Lucan. You should know what the Academy is. I trained in that building. I have never seen one commoner child come out of it. Not one. They go in, and the records end.
I looked at the six of them, asleep around my dog.
So I opened the Charter again. I had read it three times. There had to be something.
And there was. Not in the Fourth Article. In the Eleventh. A lord's household is his own. His wife. His children. His servants. And his wards.
Wards. If they're my wards, they're my household. And my household falls under the Fourth Article. No Measurer can take them without the King's own seal.
You would have to adopt them. Six peasant children. In law, you would be responsible for them. For everything, for the rest of their lives.
I'm already responsible for them.
So I wrote six wardship papers, and signed every one. And with each name, I felt a thread of cold run out of my chest, and go deeper.
Not a contract. A claim.
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter 25, coming soon.
